stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.7 key concept: the casta system in the Americas reflected new social hierarchies based on ancestry, as colonial societies combined European, African, and Indigenous peoples
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing social hierarchy in Spanish America, c. 1600–1750
stimulusBlocks.text:
Spanish American society was ranked largely by ancestry. At the top were peninsulares, people born in Spain, who held the highest offices. Below them were creoles, people of Spanish descent born in the Americas. Mestizos had mixed Spanish and Indigenous ancestry, and mulattoes had mixed Spanish and African ancestry. Indigenous people and enslaved Africans were near the bottom.

In the 1700s, painters produced casta paintings that labeled many categories of mixed ancestry. Historians note that the categories were not always fixed in practice: wealth, occupation, and reputation could change how a person was classified.

questions.prompt: The historians in the second paragraph would most likely agree that
choices: casta paintings showed society exactly as it was
casta categories mattered only in Spain
casta categories could shift with wealth and reputation
casta categories were always fixed at birth and could never change
questions.explanation: Wealth, occupation, and reputation could change classification.
choiceExplanations: Paintings labeled ideal categories, not exact practice.
The system operated in Spanish America.
Wealth, occupation, and reputation could change classification.
The historians reject fixed categories.
questions.distinguisher: The historians say categories were not always fixed in practice.

questions.prompt: Montaigne's main claim about the people of Brazil is that
choices: they should be conquered and converted
they had no customs or laws of their own
Europeans call them barbarous because they lack any religion or system of laws
Europeans call them barbarous only because their customs are unfamiliar
questions.explanation: He says everyone calls barbarism whatever is not in use in his own country.
choiceExplanations: He does not call for conquest.
He treats their customs as worth comparing with Europe's.
His point is unfamiliarity, not religion.
He says everyone calls barbarism whatever is not in use in his own country.
questions.distinguisher: Montaigne says people call barbarism whatever is not in use in their own country, not a lack of religion.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Michel de Montaigne, French writer and landowner, essay “Of Cannibals,” published in 1580, discussing the Tupinamba people of Brazil
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Essays of Montaigne, trans. Charles Cotton, ed. William Carew Hazlitt (1877), Book I, ch. 30, “Of Cannibals.” Project Gutenberg eBook #3600.
stimulusBlocks.note: Antarctic France was a short-lived French colony in Brazil founded by Villegaignon in 1555. “This nation” means the Tupinamba. The last lines refer to cruelty during France's wars of religion.
stimulusBlocks.text:
I long had a man in my house that lived ten or twelve years in the New World, discovered in these latter days, and in that part of it where Villegaignon landed, . . . which he called Antarctic France. . . .

Now, to return to my subject, I find that there is nothing barbarous and savage in this nation, by anything that I can gather, excepting, that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country. . . .

I am not sorry that we should here take notice of the barbarous horror of so cruel an action, but that, seeing so clearly into their faults, we should be so blind to our own. I conceive there is more barbarity in eating a man alive, than when he is dead; in tearing a body limb from limb by racks and torments, that is yet in perfect sense; . . . (as we have not only read, but lately seen, not amongst inveterate and mortal enemies, but among neighbours and fellow-citizens, and, which is worse, under colour of piety and religion), than to roast and eat him after he is dead.

questions.prompt: Montaigne's argument in the last paragraph is most likely shaped by
choices: his service as a Spanish colonial official
the cruelty he witnessed during the conquest of Mexico
the cruelty he witnessed during France's religious wars
his travels through the interior of Brazil
questions.explanation: He points to torture among neighbors and fellow-citizens under color of religion, meaning France's wars.
choiceExplanations: He was a French writer.
He refers to events in France.
He points to torture among neighbors and fellow-citizens under color of religion, meaning France's wars.
He learned about Brazil from a man in his house.
questions.distinguisher: He refers to cruelty among neighbors and fellow-citizens, not in Mexico.

choices: They owed tribute and labor service to the Spanish colonial officials

questions.explanation: Criollos owned land and mines but were excluded from top offices, which went to peninsulares.
choiceExplanations: Tribute and labor were owed by Indigenous peoples.
The passage says criollos owned much of the land and many mines.
Criollos owned land and mines but were excluded from top offices, which went to peninsulares.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.7 key concept: Spanish American society was organized into hierarchies based on birth and ancestry
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing social hierarchy in Spanish America, c. 1600–1750
stimulusBlocks.text:
By the 1700s, Spanish America had a social hierarchy based on birth and ancestry. At the top were peninsulares, officials born in Spain, who held the highest offices in government and the Church. Below them were criollos, people of Spanish descent born in the Americas, who owned much of the land and many mines but were barred from most top positions.

Mestizos, people of mixed Spanish and Indigenous ancestry, and mulattos, people of mixed European and African ancestry, held a lower rank. Indigenous peoples, who owed tribute and labor, and enslaved Africans ranked lower still. Officials used casta labels that recorded ancestry in detail to assign legal status, though in practice people could sometimes change their standing through wealth or marriage.

questions.prompt: The importance of birthplace and ancestry in Spanish America is best explained by
choices: Indigenous traditions of hereditary rank that the Spanish adopted
Enlightenment ideas that all people are born equal in rights
The abolition of slavery throughout the Spanish colonies by 1700
Spanish efforts to reserve power for people born in Spain
questions.explanation: A hierarchy of conquerors above those of mixed or Indigenous ancestry served to protect Spanish control of the colonies.
choiceExplanations: The hierarchy was imposed by Spanish colonial authorities.
Enlightenment equality was a challenge to the casta hierarchy, not its cause.
Slavery was not abolished in Spanish America in this period.
A hierarchy of conquerors above those of mixed or Indigenous ancestry served to protect Spanish control of the colonies.
questions.distinguisher: Indigenous societies had their own hierarchies, but the casta system was a Spanish creation.
